*: The upper motor neuron's cell body sits in layer V of the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus), hand area, opposite the limb.
Its axon leaves layer V and enters the white matter under the gyrus.
The axon descends through the corona radiata and the internal capsule‹ (lecture 10: anterior limb and genu; most texts: posterior limb)›.
It continues in the base of the cerebral peduncle of the midbrain.
It runs among the longitudinal fibres of the basis pontis.
It forms the pyramid on the ventral surface of the medulla.
About 80 % of the fibres cross the midline at the pyramidal (motor) decussation, at the junction of the medulla and the spinal cord.
The crossed fibres descend in the lateral corticospinal tract of the lateral funiculus and end on lower motor neurons in the lateral ventral horn.
The other 20 % stay on the same side and descend in the anterior corticospinal tract of the anterior funiculus.
The lower motor neuron (alpha motor neuron, lamina IX) sits in the lateral ventral horn, on the same side as the limb.
Its axon leaves the cord in the ventral root and joins the spinal nerve.
It runs in the brachial plexus and the ulnar nerve to the muscles of the hand (distal limb).
The lower motor neuron's synapse on the muscle fibres makes the hand muscles contract.
The upper motor neuron's cell body sits in layer V of the motor cortex.
Its axon descends through the internal capsule, peduncle, pons and pyramid, crosses at the motor decussation and runs down the lateral corticospinal tract.
The lower motor neuron sits in the ventral horn (lamina IX) and is the final common path to the muscle.
Its axon leaves the cord in the ventral root and joins the spinal nerve.
It runs in the brachial plexus and ulnar nerve to the hand muscles.
Damage to the upper motor neuron gives spastic weakness; damage to the lower motor neuron gives flaccid weakness.
The upper motor neuron's cell body sits in layer V of the lateral motor cortex, face area, opposite the muscles.
Its axon leaves the lateral motor cortex through the corona radiata.
It descends through the genu of the internal capsule.
It continues in the base of the cerebral peduncle.
It runs with the corticospinal fibres in the basis pontis.
The fibres leave the tract and cross the midline just above each cranial motor nucleus they reach.
The lower motor neurons sit in the cranial motor nuclei: motor V, facial, hypoglossal and nucleus ambiguus.
From the facial nucleus the facial nerve loops over the abducens nucleus, leaves the pons and runs to the muscles of the face.
The facial nerve's endings make the muscles of facial expression contract.
Motor V runs in the mandibular nerve to the masseter, XII to the tongue and the vagus from the nucleus ambiguus to the pharynx.
The masseter, tongue and pharyngeal muscles contract on the side of their nerves.

leg: Tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps and its muscle spindles.
The Ia afferent runs in the femoral nerve to the L4 dorsal root ganglion.
The sensory cell body sits in the dorsal root ganglion (the reflex is shown at L4; the knee jerk uses L3 and L4).
The Ia axon enters by the dorsal root and synapses directly on the alpha motor neuron in the ventral horn: one synapse, no interneuron.
The alpha motor neuron in the ventral horn is the efferent limb of the reflex arc.
Its axon leaves the cord in the ventral root and joins the spinal nerve.
It returns in the femoral nerve to the quadriceps.
The quadriceps contracts and the knee extends: the knee-jerk (stretch) reflex.

hand: A painful stimulus on the skin of the little finger excites the skin receptors.
The sensory axon runs in the ulnar nerve, the inferior trunk and the C8 root to its cell body.
The sensory cell body sits in the dorsal root ganglion.
The axon enters by the dorsal root and synapses on interneurons in the dorsal horn.
Spinal interneurons form the local circuit of the reflex, open to modulation from the brain.
The interneurons excite the alpha motor neurons of the flexor muscles: a polysynaptic reflex.
The alpha motor neuron sits in the ventral horn on the same side.
Its axon leaves the cord in the ventral root and joins the spinal nerve.
It runs in the brachial plexus and ulnar nerve to the flexors of the forearm.
The flexors contract and the hand is withdrawn from the stimulus.

*: The upper motor neuron's cell body sits in the red nucleus of the rostral midbrain tegmentum.
Its axons cross the midline in the midbrain tegmentum‹ (ventral tegmental decussation)›.
They descend through the brainstem tegmentum and in the rubrospinal tract of the lateral funiculus, beside the lateral corticospinal tract.
They drive lower motor neurons of the contralateral upper limb, favouring flexion.
The cell bodies sit in the tectum (superior and inferior colliculi), which respond to sights and sounds.
The axons cross the midline in the midbrain‹ (dorsal tegmental decussation)›.
They descend near the midline through the tegmentum and in the anterior funiculus of the cervical cord.
They reach lower motor neurons at cervical and upper thoracic levels that turn the head toward a sight or sound.
Upper motor neurons in the pontine and medullary reticular formation.
The pontine tract (extension of axial and limb muscles) and the medullary tract (inhibits extensor motor neurons, helps flexion) run in the anterior and lateral funiculi.
They act on lower motor neurons for posture and stepping.
Upper motor neurons in the vestibular nuclei of the medulla and caudal pons.
Their axons descend in the vestibulospinal tract of the anterior funiculus.
They drive lower motor neurons of axial and antigravity muscles for posture and righting.
The upper motor neuron sits in layer V of the trunk area of the motor cortex.
Its axon descends with the corticospinal fibres, does not cross in the medulla (the 20 %) and runs in the anterior funiculus.
It ends on lower motor neurons of the medial ventral horn, on both sides (one side shown).
The lower motor neuron's axon leaves in the ventral root to the axial muscles.
The trunk and proximal muscles contract for posture.
